| Proceedings of 55th Annual Meeting | 


The Fifty-Fifth Annual Meeting of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association, was held on Tuesday evening, May 
15th, 1906. 

At 6.30 o’clock the Board of Directors and Committee- 
men sat down to tea in the Lecture Hall and Board Room, 
served by the Ladies’ Auxiliary. ' 

After tea Mr. C. H. Goode, of Adelaide, South Australia, 
and Rey. W. J. Southam, of Hong Kong, spoke concerning 
Association work in their respective countries. 

The Annual Meeting assembled in Association Hall at 
8.15 o’clock, Mr. John W. Ross, President, in the chair. 

After devotional exercises, the report of the Membership 
Committee was read by Mr. G. A. Barrat. 

Mr. L. H. Packard, Treasurer, presented the financial 
statement, showing a balance of $66.98 on hand. 

The annual report of the Board of Directors was read 
by Mr. C. K. Calhoun. 

Mr. W. Y. King read the report of the Foreign Work 
Committee; Mr. -A. 8S. MeAlister that of the Railroad 
Branch; and Mr. Calhoun the report of the Ladies’ 
Auxiliary. 

The reports of the Religious, Social, Educational, 
Physical, Junior, and Camp Committees were presented in 
printed form and briefly commented on in order by Messrs. 
G. E. Williams, J. K. MeNutt, S. P. Leet, C. C. Holland, 
A. L. Paterson, B. S. R. Watson. On motion all the reports 
were adopted. . 

Mr. ©. T. Williams nominated the following Directors 
for the ensuing three years:—L. H. Packard, Dr. W. F. 
Hamilton, C. W. Brown, S. P. Leet, R. C. Holden, John W. 
Ross, G. F. Johnston. These were unanimously elected. 

A resolution was passed ratifying the action of the 
Board of Directors in adopting the metropolitan plan, and 
appointing a Committee of Management for the Dominion 
Square Building.

Annual Report of Board of Directors 


In presenting the Fifty-Fifth Annual Report your 
Directors would express their deep gratitude to God for the 
completion of another year of active service by the 
Association. 

The year has been notable in the following particulars :— 

The continued growth of the current work of the 
Association. 

The damage to the building by fire and its subsequent 
restoration. 

The progress made in the extension of the work in the 
city. 

The adoption of the metropolitan basis of organization. 

The second visit of Mr. Budge to Australasia. 

The passing of Sir George Williams, the founder of the 
Association movement. 


THE CURRENT WORK 


A careful review of the work carried on in the Building 
shows continued and encouraging growth. Our central 
building, as it stands to-day, although every foot of space 
has been utilized, is practically full, and at certain times of 
the year the work is carried on with great difficulty. Not- 
withstanding, the membership shows a numerical increase of 
twenty-five for the year, and a gain in receipts of $49.97. 
This result, in view of the serious disturbance caused by the 
fire, is extremely gratifying. 

The Educational Department shows a steady increase in 
enrollment, attendance, and receipts from tuition fees, 
together with splendid interest in the other features. The 
addition of a course of studies in matriculation for the 
university is a long step in advance. 

The Physical and Junior Departments report an increase 
in the volume and variety of their work, but their activities 
suffer for lack of adequate space and equipment. This con- 
dition must prevail until the new gymnasium is_ built 

oO 


ve 


providing for the growth of the physical department and 
giving the boys the unrestricted use of the present quarters. 

The social and religious work has suffered most during 
the year—the social work being practically suspended with 
the exception of the Sunday Evening Strangers’ Tea. 

The religious meetings and Bible Classes compare 
favorably with other years, and good results have been noted. 
Preparations for a larger and more aggressive work next 
year in both Bible study and evangelistic meetings are 
already well advanced. 

The financial affairs of the Association have been care- 
fully supervised by the Finance Committee, and to their 
energy and faithfulness may be attributed the favorable 
condition in which we find our current expenses at the close 
of another year. 

In February we received a bequest of $75.00 from the 
late Mr. John Bostwick, a member of the Association until 
his death, ‘‘the sum of $25.00 to be devoted to the new 
gymnasium,’’ and ‘‘$50.00 to the purchase of Bibles for the 
Gymnasium Men’s Bible Class, or for any other object 
deemed advisable by the Directors thereof.’’ 

We have recently learned of a bequest of $10,000 in 
favor of the Association under the will of the late Mr. James 
Moore, for many years a subscriber and warm friend of the 
Association. 

The Railroad Branch at Point St. Charles has continued 
to do valuable work for the railroad and other young men 
in that part of the city. On April 1st, Mr. L. P. McLennan, 
the Secretary, resigned to take charge of the Association 
at North Sydney, C.B., and was succeeded by Mr. A. S. 
MeAlister, of Island Pond. The removal of the Grand 
Trunk running shops from Point St. Charles to Turecot has 
caused a loss in membership, and will change the character 
of the work somewhat. New plans have been devised to 
meet this emergency, and an effective work for the large 
population of young men at that point will continue. 

The restoration of the Association building after the 
serious fire of June 8th last, has occupied a great deal of 
time and thought. Your Directors had in view certain 
changes in the interior of the building to be undertaken when 
the extension should be erected. The fire made it necessary 
to undertake these changes at once, and the result has been 
a rearrangement, now almost completed, affecting the 
auditorium, boys’ department, library, parlors, ete., giving 


10 


The Teaching Staff 


The Assembly Hall 


an improved equipment and utilizing our space to the best 
possible advantage. The cost of the restoration and changes 
will only partially be met by insurance, and at this date a 
balance of $5,193.30 is still to be provided for. 

The new locker room projected last year has now been 
fitted up in good style with 150 steel lockers, greatly to the 
convenience and pleasure of our members. 

In September last the Directors exercised their option 
on the front half of the vacant lot adjoining the building, 
and acquired same at a cost of $12,163.23. The entire lot 
now belongs to the Association for the extension of the 
Dominion Square building. 

The erection of an addition to the present building, 
together with the extension of the work to other points in 
the city has been kept steadily before your Directors during 
the year. The project has been delayed by the time occupied 
in restoring the building after the fire, but the changes there 
made are part of the larger plan and will not need to be 
repeated. 

To accomplish all that is desired a fund of at least 
$175,000 is considered necessary. Subscriptions aggregating 
$40,000 have been secured up to this time, and the matter 
will be actively pushed during the present year. It cannot 
be too strongly impressed upon our members that this enter- 
prise, while in no sense beyond our needs, or the ability of 
the city, is nevertheless a very large one. It will require 
the united efforts and devotion of your Directors and the 
entire membership. As soon as sufficient progress has been 
made the active co-operation of all our members will be 
invited for the completion of this task. 

As part of this plan a Committee of the Board have 
been carefully investigating conditions for the establishment 
of a branch in the east end of the city in response to urgent 
and repeated invitations from the pastors and young men 
of that section. An option has been secured on a suitable 
location, and as soon as the final choice of the site has been 
made the matter will be actively promoted. 

Your Board have also been approached by a deputation 
from the north end of the city, urging the establishment of 
a branch in that section. This also is receiving the earnest 
attention of the Board. 


METROPOLITAN ORGANIZATION 


The growth of our Association and the ealls for its 
extension in the city have made it necessary to relieve the 
Board from the detailed supervision of the work in the 
Dominion Square building in order to concentrate upon the 
larger issues of the work in the city. After careful considera- 
tion the Board have decided to adopt a plan of organization 
under which the work in the Dominion Square building will 
be entrusted to a Committee of Management consisting of 
twenty-one members, who will be responsible for the super- 
vision of the work in all its details, and will report regularly 
to the Board of Directors. The Board will continue to 
exercise general supervision at Dominion Square building, 
Point St. Charles, and such other points as may be organized 
later. Although provision for this step was made in the 
Constitution some time ago, a resolution will be presented 
this evening asking the annual meeting to endorse the action 
of the Board in this matter. 


MR. BUDGE’S VISIT TO AUSTRALIA 


The difficulty experienced by the International Com- 
mittee in finding a suitable man to go to Australia as 
Supervising Secretary, combined with the urgent need of 
several of the Australian cities, led the International 
Committee to approach your Board early last fall with the 
request that our General Secretary, Mr. D. A. Budge, be 
granted another leave of absence to visit and assist the 
Associations in New Zealand and Australia this present 
summer. After prolonged consideration your Board felt 
called upon to accede to this request, provided Mr. Budge 
felt it to be his duty to go. Notwithstanding the great 
sacrifice involved in being absent from home for such a pro- 
tracted period, Mr. Budge consented to go, sailing from San 
Francisco on March 29th, and landing at Auckland on April 
16th. He will spend the summer months visiting the 
Associations in New Zealand and Australia, returning to 
Montreal in September. The expense of this visitation will 
be borne by the Australasian Associations. 

It is an unusual tribute to the world-wide influence of 
our Association, and to the life and labors of our beloved 
Secretary that he should be called to render this far-reaching 
service to these great sister countries of the Empire. We 
are confident that in years to come it will be a matter of 
extreme satisfaction to our Association that we were thus 


13 


able to co-operate in the strengthening of Association work 
in that part of the world. 

Your Directors would take this opportunity of express- 
ing their deep appreciation of the long and remarkable 
service rendered by Mr. Budge, not only in Montreal, but in 
the Association brotherhood at large. 


DEATH OF SIR GEORGE WILLIAMS 


During the past year the Associations throughout the 
world have experienced a great loss in the death of our 
honored founder, Sir George Williams, of London, England, 
who passed away after a short illness on November 6th last, 
at the age of 84. His remains were accorded the high honor 
of interment in St. Paul’s Cathedral. A memorial service 
was held by our Association in the American Presbyterian 
Church on Sunday afternoon, November 12th, addressed by 
Rev. G. Osborne Troop, Mr. B. R. Barber, of Caleutta, and 
Mr. D. A. Budge, our General Secretary. <A fitting resolution 
of sympathy and regard was prepared and forwarded to his 
family. The Association has since had the pleasure of 
acknowledging the gift of a handsome enlarged photograph 
of Sir George suitably framed, which has been hung in our 
building as a gift from his son, Mr. Howard Williams. 

The hearty thanks of the Association are due to the 
Ladies’ Auxiliary for the very large service they have ren- 
dered during the year in connection with the various social 
occasions, and also in the furnishing of several of the 
members rooms, which they have kindly undertaken. Their 
sympathetic assistance is an encouragement in the work at 
all times. 

The following changes have taken place on our staff 
during the year :— 

Mr. J. Stuart Jamieson, of Toronto, succeeded to the 
position of Educational Director on July 1st. 

Mr. H. O. McGuire, Assistant Physical Director, 
resigned on September Ist, to enter the Springfield Training 
School, and was succeeded by Mr. Herbert Moule, of 
Charlottetown, P.E.I. 

Mr. W. J. Holliday entered the service of the 
Association on April 9th as Assistant Secretary. 

The Directors wish to record their deep appreciation 
of the faithful work performed by each member of the staff 
during the year, to Which may be attributed in a very large 
measure the suecess which has attended our efforts.

In conclusion the Directors invite the earnest co-opera- 
tion of the members in furthering the general objects of the 
Association, especially its religious work. This can never 
be left to the officers of the Association no matter how 
efficient, but is the privilege and opportunity of every member 
in extending the Master’s Kingdom. 

They would impress upon the members and _ citizens 
generally the urgent need of raising $175,000 to make pos- 
sible the enlargement of the Dominion Square building, the 


15 


increase of the Association library to at least 10,000 volumes, 
the extinction of the debt of $9,000 on the railroad men’s 
building at Point St. Charles, the purchase of land and 
erection of branch buildings in the east and north ends of 
the city. 


Respectfully submitted, 


JOHN W. ROSS, 
President. 


C. K. CALHOUN, 
Asst. General Secretary.

The total receipts for 1906 were $8,685.41, against $8,935.44 lost year, 
a gain of $49.95. The unsettled condition. of the building has made 
it difficult to secure the renewal of quite a number of our members, 
and has hindered the Committee in securing new men. Of the 733 
new members who joined during the year, 163 were active and 570 
associate; 479 boarding and 254 living at home; 412 took out regu- 
lar memberships, 321 limited. There were no sustaining memberships 
taken out in 1906.

RELIGIOUS DEPARTMENT |@3| 


The weekly meetings and Bible Classes have been held regularly, 
with the exception of the Men’s Meeting, which was seriously dis- 
turbed owing to the unfinished condition of Association Hall 
during the fall months. It became necessary to suspend this meeting 
until December, and the ground thus lost was not overtaken during the 
balance of the season. 

The Saturday evening meeting had a total attendance of 2,080, 
an average of 40 for the year. During the summer months the meet- 
ing was held in the small lecture hall upstairs, and early in the fall 
meetings were resumed in the regular lecture hall. 

The Men’s Meeting on Sunday at 4 p.m. did not commence until 
December 10th, and continued until Mareh 25th, with a total attend- 
ance for the sixteen meetings of 2,138, average 134. With the 
exception of Dr. Geo. J. Fisher, of New York, and Mr, W. P. Archi- 
bald, of Ottawa, the meetings were addressed by local pastors. Not- 
withstanding our inability to plan ahead and secure speakers from 4 
distance, as formerly, the average attendance was slightly larger than 
last year. The musical service was in charge of Mr. A. L. Paterson, 
assisted by a male chorus. 

The Sunday Afternoon Bible Class has met regularly through the 
year at 3 o’clock, with a total attendance of 3,112, an average of 60. The 
changes in the hour of meeting have affected to some extent the attend- 
ance of former members, but a good average has been obtained. 
Instead of the class being largest in the winter, as formerly, it is now 
larger in the summer months, due, doubtless, to the absence of the 
Men’s Meeting at that season of the year, and also to the larger 
number of strangers who are in the city then. 

The following visitors have spoken at the Class with great 
acceptance: Mr. Geo. C. Stebbins, Brooklyn, N.Y.; Rev. Dr. Morrison, 
Chieago; Rev. Dr. Stone, of Baltimore; Rev. Dr. W. E. Taylor, of 
Toronto; Mr. W. H. Ball, Detroit; Mr. W. P. Archibald, Ottawa. 

The Bible Classes have received a great deal of attention. Con- 
siderable progress has been made in enlarging both the number of 
classes and the attendance. A total of 16 Bible Classes were held, 
seven of these being conducted by members of the staff, and nine by} 
volunteer leaders from amongst our members, 


25 


Class in Mechanical Drawing 


One of the Class Rooms 


» 


Special endeavor has been made to develop teachers from amongst 
the members of these classes, with better success this year than at any 
time previous. 

The Tuesday Evening Bible Classes were reorganized, commencing 
November 7th, and met regularly until about April Ist. The men took 
tea together at 6,30, separating at 7.00 for the study hour. The 
thanks of the Association are again due Rey. J. L. Gilmour for leading 
a class in the study of the Acts and the Epistles. 

A very interesting and profitable conterence on Bib’e Study was 
conducted by Mr. F. S. Goodman, of New York City, on March Ist, 
which greatly enlarged the interest of our members in this (rection. 
One of the results has been the reorganization of the Bible Study 
Committee, and the formation of a new Bible Class to continue a 
seriés of studies during the summer months on Tuesday evening. This 
class will be led by members of the staff in turn. In this way we will 
be able to keep in touch with men who have been attending the 
classes during the winter, and prepare for reopening promptly on 
October Ist. 

The names of sixty-five young men were referred to pastors during 
the year. While it has been difficult to keep an accurate record, an 
encouraging number of men and boys have united with the churches 
during the year, whose interest in this respect was attributable to the 
Association. 

Short devotional services have been held at the Western Hospital 
on Sunuay morning under the leadership of several of our members, 
assisted by other friends. 

The Militia Camp work was again undertaken at Laprairie 
June 17-29, in charge of Mr. Alex, R. Ross, B.A., and Mr. W. 8S. 
Hopkins, of Sherbrooke, together with members of our own staff and 
several speakers from the city. The meetings, reading matter, games, 
an(l general privileges supplied were greatly appreciated by the men. 

The attendance at the meetings and Bible Classes for the year was

EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT 


EVENING CLASSES—October 2nd-March 31st 


Educational C:asses were conducted in fourteen subjects for men, 
and four for boys, thirty classes meeting weekly. ; 

Individual enrolment was 585, class enrolment 790. Total attend- 
ance 12,618, as against 10,833 last year. 

Total fees received this year $2,156.00, last year $1,665.05, a 
gain of $490.95, 

Total expenses this year $2,308.45, last year $2,159.50; increase 
of $148.95. ) 

Classes for the spring term will continue in seven subjects, viz., 
Bookkeeping, Typewriting, Penmanship, Shorthand, French, German, 
Matriculation, as against four last season. 

International examinations were held April 2-7 in Accountancy, 
Arithmetic, English, Bookkeeping, Shorthand, Steam Engincering, 
Hlectricity, Mechanical Drawing. Preparatory Group Course for boys, 
Reading Course No. 1 for boys. Examinations were given in ten 
subjects to 146 students, as against six subjects to 84 students last 
year, 

Juniors took these competitive examinations this year for the 
first time. One hundred and twenty-five boys studied in the classes as 
against 25 last year. Thirty-six took examinations. 

The Committee encouraged the formation of a Reading Club 
among the boys. A series of talks was given to the boys by the 
Edueational Director on History and Government, preparatory to the 
International Examinations in the Boys’ Group Course. Twenty-six 
boys attended. Seventeen took the examination in this course. 
Fifteen obtained 75 per cent. 

Another new feature was the formation of an evening class to 
prepare students in Matriculation for the University. J. G. Lorri- 
man, B.A., and W. G. McNaughton, B.A., B.Sc., were engaged as 
teachers. Eighteen employed young men have availed themselves of 
this opportunity. It is hoped that the class will continue through the 
summer months. 


DEBATING CLUB 


Membership 31. The Club met every Monday evening throughout 
the winter. In addition to programmes of debate and open discussion, 
two dinners were held where special attention was given to after- 
dinner speaking.

‘PRACTICAL TALKS 


Two series of Practical Talks, extending over the winter term, were 
an important feature of the season’s work. The Talks were of great 
practical value to young men and promoted an interest in the 
Association. .

-4| READING ROOM ano LIBRARY 


The Library was closed a great part of the year during the 
restoration of the building. Meantime, the books have been shelved 
in their new quarters, many antiquated and worn out ones discarded, 
and many standard books replaced. Two hundred and forty books 
were added. The catalogue was corrected, new shelf lists made, and 
a new charging system adopted. 

The Library contains about 4,800 volumes. During the ten weeks 
since re-opening 366 members have used its privileges, and 1,696 books 


30 


have been issued. The percentage of fiction books taken has shown 
a slight tendency to decrease from week to week.

The Reading Room contains 170 papers and magazines in the 
Senior Department, and 18 in the Junior Department. Of these 23 
were donated. 

We wish to make special acknowledgment of the gift of a very 
fine geographical globe for use in the Reference Library by Mrs. Wm. 
Neil.

viz: Papers and magazines, $299.49; magazine holders, $67.04; 
library account, $261.98.

|=8z | PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT “Ne 


Each succeeding year more clearly demonstrates that exercise is 
not merely a pastime, but a necessity to men of all ages, in all walks 
of life. The work of the past year has been conducted along the 
same lines as before and a healthy growth is noted in the different 
activities of the Department. Early in the fall the different classes 
were organized, each having its own chairman and secretary. These 
organized groups have had a helpful influence upon the work in 
general, and their own classes in particular. Thé installation of 150 
large steel lockers in the new locker-room has met a long-felt need, 
and is greatly appreciated, especially by the business men. 

Dr. Geo. J. Fisher, Secretary of the Athletic League of North 
America, made us a very helpful visit early in January, at which 
time he addressed four groups of our members. Mr. J. H. Crocker, of 
Toronto, visited us and spoke on the occasion of the Fifth Annual 
Physical Department Banquet. 

A valuable addition to our work has been the forming of an 
Intermediate Leaders’ Corps, similar to the Senior Leaders’ Corps, 
and in a sense a course preparatory to their becoming Senior 
Leaders. The men in this group have rendered excellent service to 
the Association. Mr, Allan McLeod is President. 


31 


Class in Electricity 


. 
For the Typewriting Class 


Classes in Physica] Training have been conducted by our mem at 
the following places: Fairmount Young Men’s Association; Railroad 
Branch; Inspector Street Mission; St. Jude’s Church; Mackay 
Institute, and Lachine. This extension of our work outside the build- 
ing is an important development. 

Seven hundred and forty-four class sessions were conducted, with 
a total attendance of 17,921, an average of over 2,300 per month and 
a gain in gross attendance for the year of 1,950. Seven hundred and 
eighty-three men and boys registered in 26 weekly classes. The 
detaiied statement of attendance is as follows:

Four hundred and fifty-two were physically or medically examined. 
About 1,200 different members used the department during the season. 
Through the kindness of Dr. H. B. Cushing, an excellent course of 
lectures, ‘‘ First Aid to the Injured,’’ was conducted, with an average 
attendance of 23. Ten members took the St. John’s Ambulance Corps 
Examinations, nine of whom passed. The Committee record their 
sincere appreciation of the valuable services rendered by Dr. F. W. 
Gilday and Dr. H. B. Cushing as medical examiners. 

The department conducts eleven athletic clubs, with a membership 
of over 500. 


LEADERS 


The Leaders’ Corps report a membership of 22. Messrs. Fred. 
Mann, A. H. Cross, and A. Stewart were elected as new Leaders. 

Instead of the annual banquet, a reception was given to Physical 
Department members on March 8th. This proved a good step, not 


33 


only promoting a social spirit in the Corps, but being of value to the 
Association as a whole. 

The following Leaders conducted classes in different places in the 
city: Messrs. F. W. Shaw, H. H. Field, Fred Mann, Geo, Burton, 
Alex. Stewart, S. R. Hall, H. S. Greenleese, A. G. Budge. 


HARRIER CLUB 


Had a most successful season, and were proud to win the five-mile 
Harrier Championship of Canada, competed for at Ottawa in Septem- 
ber. This victory created quite an interest amongst the membership 
and we are looking forward this year to a similar victory, and to 
retaining the beautiful Dunlop trophy in our cabinet for another year. 

Our runners were unfortunate in the City and District meets, losing 
the championship in both the Senior and Junior races owing to the 
fact that some of our best runners were unable to compete. 

Week-night handicaps were held during the summer, and proved 
helpful in keeping up the interest at that time. 


BOWLING 


Has not been so successful this year, due to the fact that a num- 
ber of our best bowlers have left for other organizations with better 
alleys. We have spent the time in teaching new men to bowl. As we 
have but two alleys we are unable to enter a regular city league. 
Therefore, the Committee were instrumental in organizing an indepen- 
dent league in the city, composed of five different clubs. Home and 
home matches were rolled, and our team succeeded in winning the 
championship of this league. Weekly competitions have been held, 
and prizes given for the highest single score, and the highest average 
score. We hope that soon the Association will be able to offer us new 
alleys. 


HOCKEY 


Owing to inability to secure proper ice accommodation, this Club 
was not active the past season, 


BASKETBALL 


Five teams were entered in the Senior League and four in the 


. Intermediate, representing 72 different players. The teams were 


evenly matched and the spirit of play excellent. This year the Asso- 
ciation adopted the Canadian Basketball Rules and the Committee feel 
that these rules made the game faster and cleaner. 

The Britts tied with the Tigers in the Senior Championship, and 
the Beavers tied with the Stars in the Intermediate series. In the 
play off the Britts and the Beavers won in their respective series. 

At the close of our season the City Basketball League was formed, 
in which the Association had a large part. We entered two teams in 
the Senior and one in the Intermediate. Our two teams finished first 
and second in the Senior series, thereby winning the city championship 
for the Association. The, Intermediate team finished second. 

Outside teams played in our gymnasium from McGill, Westmount, 
M. A. A. A., Railroad Y. M. C. A., and Quebee. 


34 


BASEBALL 


The past season was one of the best in the history of the Club. 
Although we did not win the city championship, the games were well 
contested, clean sport was played and a fine spirit shown by the men. 
The Association was instrumental in organizing the Mount Royal 
Amateur Baseball League, controlling all amateur baseball in the city. 
This league has an executive of three men who have entire charge of 
league matters for the season. Our secretary was a member of that 
executive. 

During the early season the practices were well attended. 

The Club greatly appreciates the Association securing for them the 
Montreal Baseball grounds, 

Membership 22. 


TENNIS 


The past year has been most successful. The courts were put in 
condition early, and kept in good condition well into September. 
The evening attendance averaged 18. Our membership was 42. 


SNOWSHOE 


This Club reports a good season. The outings were less numerous 
owing to lack of snow. 

The annual reception in December was the best and largest held 
by the Club. Our membership was 72. 


FOOTBALL 


The Football Club entered two teams in the City League, one 
Senior and one Intermediate, and for a young Club made a remarkably 
good showing. Membership was 34. This Club hopes to win the 
championship in both series the coming season. 


ATHLETIC CLUB 


The Field Day was held on the M. A. A. A. grounds, September 
23rd. There were 42 individual entries and the events were well con- 
tested. Two Association records were broken, viz., the mile and half- 
mile, both by George Palmer. 

The presentation of prizes took place in the gymnasium in the 
evening after the games. 


BIBLE STUDY CLUB 


The Gymnasium Mer’s Bible Study Club, during the past year, 
has been studying Bible Characters. For the past four years this 
Club has been conducted as a unit. In the middle of this year it was 
decided to divide the Club into groups, securing for each group a 
teacher from the Bible Study Club Committee. This was done with 
helpful results and, while the attendance has not increased, better work 
has been done, more men interested, and certain men have attended 
who could not have been reached in any other way. 

The total attendance for the year was 1,081, average 34. The 
Club held 32 sessions and enrolled 84 different men. The foundation 
has been laid this year for a larger work during 1906-07. 

C. C. HOLLAND, 
Chairman. 
35 


The work of the Committee has been regularly carried on, and 
whenever possible the visits of the Foreign Secretaries of the Inter- 
national Committee, on furlough in Amercia, have been availed of, 
to draw inspiration and enthusiasm therefrom, and much help has 
been derived in this way from addresses given to large gatherings 
by Mr. B. R. Barber, of Caleutta, India, and Mr, V. W. Helm, of 
Tokio, Japan. The latter illustrated his address with lantern slides 
relating to the Russo-Japanese War—of intense interest. 

Over $300 has been sent, through members of the Association, for 
work amongst the Japanese soldiers, and our help has been much 
appreciated. 

Encouraging reports are received from Mr. Chas, 8. Paterson, 
regarding the work amongst the High School Boys of Caleutta. Thé 
progress of the work does not seem to have been to any extent retarded 
by the ‘‘ boycott,’’ established by the native Bengalese, against the 
English government officials, and naturally also Europeans generally, 
through the unpopular division of the Province of Bengal by the 
authorities. The interest and attendance of the native boys seemingly 
has been regained and retained,

During the month of November, owing to lack of accommodation 
in our locker rooms and gymnasium, no regular tickets were issued to 
business boys. Those who wished to join the gymnasium had to take 
out a limited ticket and wait for the non-renewal of some regular 
member, With our present equipment it is impossible to landle more 
than 350 boys in the Evening Classes. 


RELIGIOUS 


The Friday Evening Meeting has been held regularly throughout 
the year, with the exception of the month of July. This meeting is 
attended by boys between the ages of 14 and 138, three-quarters of the 
number being from 16 to 18 years of age. The average attendance 
for the year has been 35, the same as last year. 

The school boys between the ages of 11 and 14 have been formed 
into a Bible Study Club with officers and committeemen elected from 
the boys themselves. They preside at the meeting and ask the 
Secretary to lead in the lesson. The enro’ment in this class is 75, with 
an average attendance of 36. 

In order to carry out the social side of the Club, snowshoe tramps, 
banquets, game tournaments, and socials were given by the Club each 
month, only those who had attended three out of the four classes held 
during the month receiving invitations. A manly, Christian spirit has 
been engendered, the value of which it is impossible to overestimate. 

More than 285 boys have been in attendance at these two meect- 
ings, and at least 70 per cent. of that number have attended half the 
meetings held during the season. 

The Song Services have been held every second Sunday morning 
at the Montreal General Hospital from October to May. The average 
attendance has been 28. 

The fol'owing Bible Classes have been conducted in addition to 
the meetings mentioned above:

Thirty boys took the International Examinations in Bible Study, 
only three of whom failed to pass. 

Subscriptions have been made to the Foreign Work Fund. The 
Chairman of this Committee, together with six others, will attend the 
Older Boys’ Conference at Silver Bay this summer. 

The Committee in charge of the Junior School Boys’ Class have 
written to Mr. C, S. Paterson, asking him to give the names of two 
young men whom they can support by their funds, and who will com- 
municate with the Committee from time to time. 


PHYSICAL 


The attendance at the Gymnasium Classes is included in the 
Physical Department Report. 

A new organization has been formed this year in the Intermediate 
Leaders’ Corps, composed of 14 Christian young men between the 
ages of 15 and 20. They have a distinct organization with constitu- 
tion and by-laws, officers, and committeemen like the Senior Leaders’ 
Corps. With two exceptions, the members of this Corps are High 
School boys. They are responsible for the personal work of the Boys’ 
Department. 

Three of the Corps taught Bible Classes during the winter, and 
eight of the Corps are taking the normal course in preparation for 
teaching Bible Classes next season. The success of the work in every 
department is largely due to their untiring efforts. 

The Summer Camp at Lac St. Joseph, under the leadership of Mr, 
J. E. Merritt, Physical Director, was enjoyed by 48 boys. The Bible 
Classes, the companionship of Christian men, and the general healthy 
atmosphere of the Camp, caused a marked change for the better in the 
lives of many of the boys, 

Two talks on ‘‘Physical Training’’ to the boys of the city were 
given by Mr. Merritt. At the first the attendance was 160 and at the 
second 250. This large number represented every section of the city. 

A concert and gymnastic exhibition was given by the Leaders’ 
Corps, an admission fee of fifteen cents being charged. Three 
hundred of the parents and friends attended. The receipts, 
amounting to $37.80, are to help pay the expenses of a delegation to 
the Older Boys’ Conference at Silver Bay, Lake George, on August 
25th. 


EDUCATIONAL 


A report of the Evening Classes is given by the Edueational 
Department. 

Owing to the disturbed condition of the building, the boys have 
had no library this season. The magazines in the reading room have 
been used more than in previous years. 

Thirty-two boys took the International Examinations with the 
view of obtaining the McBurney Cup. 

Owing to the large increase in the membership of the Department 
over previous years, the social and religious work has been divided 
into four distinct sections. By this means we have not had the large 
mass work as formerly, but the smaller group work which has proved 
of infinitely greater value. 

The Ladies’ Committee, under the leadership of Mrs. John W. 
Ross, have rendered very efficient service. They have made the boys 
feel at home, and their willingness and forethought have contributed 
in a large measure to the success which has attended the different 
social functions, ” 


38 


Two of the Leaders’ Corps have conducted Physical Work for 
boys at Inspector Street Mission. 

Two hundred parents of the boys attended the Gymnasium 
Closing, many of whom remained for a social half-hour in the Associa- 
tion Hall at the close of the programme. 

Taken as a whole our work this season has been greatly b‘essed. 

We have had a larger Bible Class Work, an increased attendance 
at our Gymnasium Classes, and a gentlemanly, earnest spirit pervading 
the Department. 

Respectfully submitted, 


A. L. PATERSON, 
Chairman, 


PSiZ| SOCIAL DEPARTMENT [XA 


The plans of this Department, as mentioned in the report for last 
year, have not been fully carried out, on account of the fire which 
took place in the building during the early part of last summer; so 
that, except for the past four, months, it has not been possible to do 
much work of a social nature. 

The Thanksgiving Dinner and New Year’s Day Reception were 
reluctantly abandoned, on account of the unprepared state of the 
rooms; but we were able to arrange for the usual New Year’s Concert, 
which passed off successfully. 

Members’ Meetings were held on the 8th of February and 20th of 
March. Short musical programmes were carried out at these meet- 
ings and informal reports of different phases of Association work were 
presented. On the latter date, the members were given an opportunity 
of saying ‘‘Good-bye’’ to Mr. Budge, who, on that evening, left for 
Australia and New Zealand. 

On Easter Monday, a concert was given by the Turner-Weaver- 
Blair Concert Company, which proved very enjoyable and was fairlly 
well attended. 

The Sunday Afternoon Strangers’ Tea was served fortnightly 
during the season, furnishing an opportunity of meeting in a social 
way about 275 young men from different countries, many of whom 
have become members of the Association. 

The Glee Club had a successful season under the leadership of 
Mr. A. L. Paterson. During the season, the Club has rendered yalu- 
able assistance at several social gatherings and also took part in a 
most successful concert which was held on the 23rd of April. 


JAMES K. McNUTT, 
Chairman. 
EMPLOYMENT 


The Employment Bureau has been conducted during the year on 
much the same lines as formerly. Eight hundred and twenty applica- 
tions were filed and 219 situations filled. 

The Bureau has been of great assistance to young men coming as 
strangers to the city, many of whom have afterwards become members 
of the Association. 


39 


Se SUMMER CAMP Sr 
ZN ZI MASS 


Our Victoria Day party was smaller than usual, owing to the 
holiday coming in the middle of the week. About fifteen were out, 
and the fishing was good. Mr. Harry McGuire, Assistant Physical 
Director, was in charge. 

The Senior Camp opened on July 15th and closed September 5th. 
There was an attendance during the year of 103 men, an increase of 
20 per cent. over the previous year. We consider it to have been one 
of the most successful Camps we have ever held. Camp sports, the 
annual regatta, fishing, and many impromptu coneerts filled in the 
time for the campers. The Committee were fortunate in having Mr. 
P. A. Doig take charge for the entire season, and this did away with 
many difficulties which have generally been consequent on necessary 
changes. The Committee deeply appreciate the interest he has shown 
in Camp matters and the very efficient manner in which he has dealt: 
with the various problems. The Sunday services, usually led by the 
Secretary in charge, were well attended and have been much appreciated, 
most of the summer visitors around the lake coming over to attend 
them. We are indebted to Professor Caldwell, of McGill University, 
and Judge Knapp, of New York State, for the help given. We also 
had the pleasure of a visit from Mr. W. H. Ball, of Detroit, one of 
the founders of our Camp. 

A Labor Day fishing competition was held with about twenty 
competitors. The winners received their prizes at the Campers” 
Banquet. 

The First Annual Campers’ Banquet was held in November, at 
which about ninety sat down. The evening proved a success. 

A new departure this year has been the holding of a Campers’ Bible 
Class throughout the winter. The attendance and interest has been 
marked and we trust that this will only be the beginning of similar 
classes. 

Through the generosity of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Knox we were made 
the recipients of a fine wharf early in the season, which was very, 
greatly appreciated by the Campers, 

Financially we had a good year. After paying all bills we had a 
balance of $245.17, which was transferred to the Permanent Camp 
Account for the repair and upkeep of the property. 

Our urgent needs for next year are the following: Twenty mat- 
tresses; three boats; repairs to all the tents; boat-house; old ice-house 
placed near kitchen. 

B. 8. R. WATSON, 


Chairman.

In glancing over the record of the past year, which somehow seems 
to have been a shorter one than usual, the members of the Women’s 
Auxiliary very naturally ask themselves the question, have we made 
profitable use of our opportunities along the lines for which our 
organization came into being, and has the work of the Association 
here been strengthened and helped through our instrumentality? 

.In some respects the year’s work has been unlike that of previous 
ones; and we feel as though less had been accomplished than we had 
hoped, yet find comfort in the knowledge that it has not been from 
lessening of zeal or flagging of interest that results are less apparent. 

The Annual Meeting was held on May 3rd, 1905, election of officers 
resulting as follows:— 


President—Mrs. Henry Birks. 

1st Vice-President—Mrs. L. Cushing. 
2nd Vice-President—Mrs. W. Tees. 
Treasurer—Mrs. E. B. Busteed. 
Secretary—Mrs. Godbee Brown. 


Convenors of Committees— 


Social—Mrs. Budge. 
Furnishing—Mrs, Peter Laing. 
Junior—Mrs. John W. Ross. 
Finance—Mrs. Chas. Cushing. 
Flower—Mrs. John MeKergow. 


Eight business meetings have been held, with an average attend- 
ance of 15, slightly less than that of last year, to be accounted for by 
the absence of the young ladies from the monthly meetings. 

As the several Committees are reporting their work for the year 
in full, it is needless to add anything except this, that in every 
department faithful service has been cheerfully rendered. 

Perhaps the work of the Social Committee, both senior and junior, 
deserves most the word of praise, for the members of this Committee 
have been ‘‘in labors more abundant’’ almost from the opening of the 
year until its close. The many and growing demands upon this branch 
of our work make necessary the enlargement of the Social Committee 
in the near future, so that responsibility may be divided, that it rest 
not too heavily upon the few who have thus far borne the burden, often, 
literally—‘‘the heat of the day.’’ 

One social event has been omitted during the year, i.e., the New 
Year’s reception, owing to the unfinished condition of the building. 

In November your Secretary had the honor to represent this 
Auxiliary at the Provincial Convention of Women’s Auxiliaries, held 
in Toronto. This proved to be a time of inspiration and profit, and 
we hope to carry into effect some valuable suggestions gleaned from 
the many offered there. 


41 


A feature of the year’s work has been the revision of our 
Constitution, which had somewhat outlived its usefulness. Much 
thought and care have been bestowed upon this work, and we trust that 
the new Constitution, copies of which we hope to place in the hands 
of every subscriber, may enable us to do more thoroughly, and in a 
businesslike manner, the work committed to our charge. Amongst 
other changes made, the throwing open of our Annual Meeting to all 
subscribers and friends may be noticed. 

Another slight departure from the regular routine has been the 
soliciting of special subscriptions towards the purchase of rugs for 
the parlors—besides the money return thus brought, we hope to retain 
the interest thus temporarily, and in many cases, for the first time, 
awakened in our work. 

The retirement from our ranks of Mrs. Peter Laing has created a 
gap not easily filled, but we have not given up hope that some time 
ere long she may be with us again. Mrs. L. Cushing has acceptably 
filled the position left vacant by Mrs. Laing’s resignation. 

As will be shown in the report of the Furnishing Committee, 
there are good and sufficient reasons why the work done in this 
department is not more evident. 

The rapid growth of work in the Boys’ Department bids fair to 
tax the resources of the Junior Committee to the utmost, and to aid 
in this most important branch, where the future leaders of Association 
work are being primarily trained, the Auxiliary as a whole pledges its 
sympathy and support. To this end plans are on foot for the com- 
fortable fitting up of the parlors on the lower floor, which are now 
devoted to the sole use of the boys. 

With thankfulness that we have been permitted to do something 
in His name for the young men and boys of our city, and a hopeful 
outlook upon the future of the work. 

Respectfully submitted, 
CHARLOTTE E. BROWN, 
Secretary. 

Twenty-nine new names have been added to the roll during the 
past year, making a total membership of 158, against 137 of the 
previous year. 

Three. names were removed by death, Mrs. Yuile, Mrs. Boyd, and 
Miss Holt. Five names were dropped by removal of members from 
the city and other reasons unknown.
